Pasteur Institute of India (PII), Coonoor
4.1 The Institute started functioning as an autonomous body under the Ministry of Health and
Family Welfare, with effect from the 10th February, 1977. Established exclusively to treat dog-bite
victims, in the pre-independence era, the Institute has come a long way. Today, the following
activities are undertaken at the Institute:
• Production of DPT group of vaccine for EPI programme.
• Production of Tissue Culture Anti-rabies Vaccine for humans.
• Training programmes and post-graduate programmes.
• Providing consultancy services to other Institutions within the country and abroad.
• WHO collaborating centre for training in Rabies Vaccine Production and Quality Control.
• Extending academic programme for PhD affiliated to Bharathiar University, Coimbatore
and M.D. (Microbiology) affiliated to Tamil Nadu Dr. M.G.R. Medical University, Madras.
• Continuous in-house Research and Development on existing vaccine produced by the
Institute. The Institute also offers training programmes to University students pursuing
Medicine, Pharmacy, Microbiology, Biochemistry and other related subjects.
4.2 The Institute was inspected on the 9th and 10th August, 2007 by a joint inspecting team
of WHO-NRA as per the provisions of rule 78 (d) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. The
inspecting team had found deficiencies concerning the building structure, haphazard arrangement of
the rooms in the manufacturing areas without any uni-flow system of men and material for
production activities, haphazard storage, unhygienic condition found in tetanus areas, non-
classification of production areas and non-separation of critical production activity, critical
deficiencies in manufacturing practices, quality control and testing practices.
4.3 On the 3rd January, 2008 a second team visited to observe whether the defects pointed out
earlier had been rectified by the Institute. The Institute in its reply dated 4th January, 2008 to the

8
show cause notice issued by the office of Directorate General of Health Services (Drugs Control
Division) had stated that it would not be possible to completely rectify all the deficiencies especially
those relating to structure and manpower and could instead try their level best to rectify the
deficiencies within their limits. However, the CLAA suspended the manufacturing license of the unit
in January, 2008.
4.4 Subsequently, the Expert Committee under the chairmanship of the DCGI visited the
Institute from 10th and 12th July, 2008. It has been stated in the Expert Committee Report that
the modifications carried out planned in the existing set-up as well as proposal made in connection
with the new infrastructure, comply with GMP norms. The report states that the Institute has made
some efforts to renovate the old facilities and up till now they have spent Rs. 4.84 crores for the
modification. It is pertinent to note that holistic and assured approach towards renovation and GMP
compliance has not yet been adopted by the Institute. Therefore, if the facilities fall short of GMP
requirements in certain aspects even after renovation, then it may not be an assured move to
renovate old facilities for attaining the intended purpose.
5. The Committee, after going through all the details and the discussions held with the
Directors of the three vaccine producing PSUs as also the Secretary, Department of Health and
Family Welfare has the following observations/recommendations to make:
5.1 The Committee finds from the information furnished by the Ministry that while CRI,
Kasauli and BCG VL, Chennai have been functioning as subordinate offices under the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the PII, Coonoor, functions as an autonomous
institution under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. It observes that all these
Institutes, since their establishment, have remained in the public sector with the Ministry
as the nodal administrative and supervising agency. However, it is astonishing to find that
the building structures of these 100-year old institutions have continued to remain in their
original set up. Ideal position would have been to revamp the existing structures so as to
ensure their normal functioning as well as further expansion/strengthening in accordance
with the changing times/requirements. The Committee is not aware whether any initiative,
whatsoever, was taken either by the Ministry or the Director General Health Services to
draw up an action plan and take follow-up action in a time-bound manner.
5.2 The Committee would like to state here that the concept of Schedule ‘M’, which is
the Indian version of cGMP norms of WHO was mooted in 2001 and notified in 2005. Given
that the Director General Health Services is the administrative authority under which CRI,
Kasauli and BCG VL, Chennai are functioning as subordinate offices, and office of DCGI
is the nodal agency entrusted with the responsibility of ensuring cGMP compliance at PII,
Coonoor, it is the Ministry which should have made timely and appropriate efforts to
convert these age old structures as per Schedule M compliant standards. From the feedback
made available to the Committee, it can only conclude that no initiative was attempted for
drawing out an Action Plan for making these Institutes cGMP compliant. The Ministry’s
responsibility did not end with simply bringing out the required legislation in accordance
with the international norms. Rather, the real work was to begin thereafter which
unfortunately never happened. It is also not clear as to whether the Ministry has allocated
adequate funds to these Institutes for the purpose. The Committee also fails to understand
as to how the Ministry would ensure cGMP compliance in the private Institutes when it
cannot enforce the same in its own Institutes.
5.3 The Committee observes that the Ministry has failed to play the role of coordinator
and facilitator in the matter. It would like to draw attention to one such situation that
confirms its stand. From the Status note submitted by the Ministry, the Committee finds
that a proposal for converting the triple-vaccine manufacturing laboratory at CRI, Kasauli

9
into a cGMP compliant structure was made way back in 1997-98, when M/s HSCC, Noida was
awarded the contract to build a cGMP compliant structure at CRI. However, the entire
exercise ended in a failure, as M/s HSCC, Noida, after continuing the exercise for nine
years and spending Rs. 11.86 crores of public money on the project, expressed its inability
and disinterest in completing the project in December, 2006. The Committee fails to
understand the logic why the Ministry waited so long in such a crucial matter. The
Committee feels that the Ministry should have taken immediate appropriate steps such as
canceling the contract of M/s HSCC, Noida and asked other parties with technical
competence to complete the project. It epitomizes the cavalier fashion with which the
Ministry has treated the issue. Only achievement seems to be an expenditure of Rs. 11.86
crores by M/s HSCC, Noida, without any specification thereof. The Committee views with
serious concern the admission on the part of M/s HSCC, Noida about their not having any
expertise to construct a scientific structure of cGMP standards.
5.4 The Committee was informed that a Departmental Inquiry in the matter was
presently going on. The Committee observes that this matter has been hanging on for more
than ten years. More than two years have elapsed since the Project authorities have
comfortably withdrawn themselves. The inquiry also seems to be continuing in a comfortable
mode. Nobody seems to be bothered about the loss of public money and also the institute
not getting the required renovation. The Committee would appreciate if the enquiry
proceedings are completed expeditiously and full details of follow up action taken for fixing
up the responsibility against the concerned official(s) in the Ministry and imposing of
penalty on the project authority are apprised to it. The Committee can only emphasise that
the major responsibility of making these Institutes cGMP compliant lies with the Ministry
and holding the Institutes entirely responsible for the same goes against the principle of
natural justice. The Committee is of the firm opinion that the Ministry is responsible to a
large extent for the prevailing unsatisfactory situation in all the three Institutes which
resulted in the cancellation of their vaccine producing licenses and thereby leading to
shortage of life saving vaccines with serious impact on Universal Immunization Programme
and child healthcare programmes in the country.
5.5 The Status Note also informs that the Institutes suffer from acute shortage of
personnel especially in Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ in CRI, Kasauli and BCG VL, Chennai which are
subordinate offices under the office of DGHS. The vacancies stated above are reflected in
percentage in the table given below:

10
earnest by the Ministry to fill up these vacancies. The Committee has also observed that
a number of posts have either lapsed/abolished or proposed to be lapsed/abolished. The

which is an autonomous body functioning under the Ministry has not reported any shortage
of manpower. The Committee believes that if similar administrative autonomy had been
delegated to CRI and BCG VL, the problems relating to shortage of manpower and many
other such issues could have been sorted out early. The Committee would appreciate if a

earliest both at CRI and BCG VL so as to have a viable set up there.

and steam system, manufacturing area, documentation, training of personnel, self

that on the remaining ten deficiencies either corrective action has already been initiated or

5.11 The Committee would also like to mention here that neither of the inspecting team–

11
5.12 The Committee was also given to understand that the international health agency–WHO,
had offered to upgrade the technology at these three PSUs. However, the Ministry had
declined the offer and preferred to cancel their vaccine-producing license. The Committee
wonders as to why, being a member of the WHO, the Ministry did not prefer to take their
help to upgrade the technology and make these units conform to international standards.
The Committee observes that such lapses on the part of the Ministry only point out that
it has failed miserably in upgrading these units to the required standards.
5.13 The Ministry has informed that the licenses for manufacture of vaccines by CRI,
Kasauli, BCG VL, Chennai and PH, Coonoor were suspended by the DCG (I) under the
powers vested with the Central License Approving Authority (CLAA) under rule 85 (1) of
the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 which reads as under:
“The Central Licensing Approving Authority may, after giving the licensee an
opportunity to show cause why such an order should not be passed, by an order in writing
stating the reasons therefor, cancel a license issued under this part, or suspend it for such
period as he thinks fit either wholly or in respect of any of the drugs to which it relates
(or direct the licensee to stop manufacture, sale or distribution of the said drugs and
(thereupon order the destruction of drugs and) the stock thereof in the presence of an
Inspector) if in his opinion, the licensee has failed to comply with any of the conditions
of the licensee or with any provisions of the Act or rules made thereunder.”
The Committee is of the opinion that as provided in the aforesaid rule, the licenses
of these three units should have been suspended for a specific period. This period could
have been utilised for removal of all the shortcomings in a time-bound manner under the
overall supervision of the Ministry. This was the right course of action not only in
accordance with the law but also due to the fact that quite a few drawbacks have already
been removed inspite of the constraints being faced by these institutes.
5.14 The Committee also takes note of another disturbing development taking place after
the suspension of manufacturing licenses of the three Institutes. An Expert Committee was
constituted by the Ministry on the 11th April, 2008 for the assessment of the three Institutes.
The scope and terms of reference of the Expert Committee are self-revealing. Out of the
eight terms of reference of the Expert Committee, the foremost two are as follows:—
(i) Study of infrastructure facilities available at the three vaccine manufacturing
units and explore feasibility of conversion of existing laboratories into testing
laboratories or training units.
(ii) Scope of re-deployment of the existing staff in production units to the proposed
testing labs in view of the stoppage of production of vaccines.
The above terms of reference clearly indicate that the Ministry had already taken a
decision for final stoppage of vaccine production at the Institutes inspite of the fact that the
manufacturing license of the three institutes remained suspended till the time of
discrepancies noticed were finally removed. The Committee expresses its serious reservation
on this development. It is very clear that the three institutes fulfilling the vaccine
requirement of the country for the past so many decades were not given a fair chance. They
did not deserve such a treatment at the hands of their administrative Ministry.
5.15 It has also come to the notice of the Committee that after the show-cause notice
issued to the BCG VL regarding cancellation of its license on the 14th December, the DCG (I)
conveyed the proceedings of the CLAA suspending the license of BCG VL until the new
facilities were ready. On 20th February, 2008 the DCG (I) informed the Institute that

12
products manufactured at the Institute cannot be used for immunization purpose due to
non-conformities of GMP and hence, sought a proposal for destruction and writing off of the
stock lying with it.
5.16 The Committee would like to State here that until the inspections were carried out,
the Institute had been meeting the requirement of BCG vaccine for the entire country and
the same were supplied to the various States under the UIP without reports of any adverse
effects from the use of such vaccines. On the other hand, if the vaccines supplied under
the UIP conformed to the standards of safety, efficacy and quality, then what could be the
logic to order the destruction and writing off of the stock by the DCGI. The Committee
observes that since BCG VL was the sole manufacturer of BCG Vaccine in the country, such
a move could lead to shortage of vaccines across the States, thereby, affecting the Universal
Immunization Programme. The Committee’s apprehensions have been confirmed by media
reports regarding shortage of vaccines across the States. The Committee apprehends that
large amounts of vaccines produced at CRI and PH would have also met with a similar fate.
The Committee observes that the Ministry has not approached the issue with enough
foresight to ensure adequate and steady supply of vaccines and that such a move puts it in
poor light.

while for others it may be either closed or upgrading itself to cGMP standard. The
Committee is however, not convinced by the Ministry’s stand. It is clear from the submitted
lists that the Ministry is unaware whether Biological E. Pvt. Ltd. is functional as it has not
received report regarding the same in the last two years. The Committee fails to understand
how the situation could change over night and the above mentioned vaccine producing unit
could qualify all the required norms of schedule M. The Committee would like to note here
that either the Ministry had failed to provide complete information on the unit or had
chosen not to do so. In either case, it is of the opinion that more transparency in the
matter is required. The Committee is not aware about the status of private units with which
the Vaccine Procurement Cell (VPC) has placed the orders. The Committee would like to
be apprised as to whether all these units are cGMP compliant.
5.19 Another pertinent issue that draws the Committee’s attention is the procurement
price of the vaccines. The Committee believes that since the CRI, Kasauli, BCG VL,
Chennai and PH, Coonoor are in the public sector, vaccines were available to the people at
cheap price, but once the manufacturing goes into the private hands there is every
likelihood that the cost of the vaccines could go up in future, thus, defeating the very
objective of providing highly essential drugs like vaccines to the people at affordable prices.
5.20 The Committee earlier discussed that the international health agency – WHO, had
offered to upgrade the technology at the three PSUs. The Committee recommends that the

14
Ministry should explore this avenue as an alternative to build these units conforming to
international Good Manufacturing Practices.
5.21 The Committee has also been informed that a vaccine park is being proposed to be
set up in Chegalpattu near Chennai. On a specific query in this regard, the Committee was
informed that the proposed vaccine park would be in the public sector. It would be a unit
that would be established by Hindustan Latex Ltd., a public sector undertaking under the
administrative control of the Ministry. The Committee would like to point out that with
three vaccine manufacturing units already functioning for the last so many decades, the
right course of action would have been to make sincere efforts for their revamping in
accordance with the changing times. Vaccine Park coming up at the cost of already existing
units cannot be considered justified from any point of view. The Committee observes that
this project could take a couple of years before manufacturing and supply of vaccines could
actually take place. Till such time the Committee feels that procuring the country’s
requirements of various vaccines from the private sector could only increase the cost of the
vaccines thereby, adversely hitting the Exchequer. Moreover, a single centralized vaccine
producing park may not be able to cater to the needs of the billion plus and growing
population of the country.
5.22 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should revoke the
suspension of vaccine manufacturing licenses of the three vaccine producing PSUs at the
earliest. Until such time that new infrastructures are built conforming to the Schedule M
norms, these Institutes may be allowed to continue production in the old structures after
carrying out the rectifications either fully or to the extent possible. The Committee would
like to point out that all the three units have their own quality control system. Not only
this National Quality Control Authority is also involved in the quality control of vaccines
produced by these units. In such a scenario, there is little likelihood of non-standard
vaccines being produced by them. These Institutes may be allowed the time sought by them
as also provided with adequate funds for completing the rectification works but it should be
done under the aegis of the Ministry so that they do not exceed the time-frame.
5.23 The Committee also recommends that all the vacancies in all cadres should be filled
up at the earliest and the recruitments rules for those posts, which are yet to be framed,
should be framed immediately. The Committee further recommends that the existing
scientific and technical staff should be given appropriate training to make them cGMP
compliant. The Committee is not aware about the status of private units with which the
Vaccine Procurement Cell (VPC) has place the orders. The Committee would like to be
apprised as to whether all these units are cGMP compliant.

15
OBSERV ATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee finds from the information furnished by the Ministry that while CRI,
Kasauli and BCG VL, Chennai have been functioning as subordinate offices under the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the PII, Coonoor, functions as an autonomous
institution under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. It observes that all these
Institutes, since their establishment, have remained in the public sector with the Ministry
as the nodal administrative and supervising agency. However, it is astonishing to find that
the building structures of these 100-year old institutions have continued to remain in their
original set up. Ideal position would have been to revamp the existing structures so as to
ensure their normal functioning as well as further expansion/strengthening in accordance
with the changing times/requirements. The Committee is not aware whether any initiative,
whatsoever, was taken either by the Ministry or the Director General (Health Services) to
draw up an action plan and take follow-up action in a time-bound manner. (Para 5.1)
The Committee would like to state here that the concept of Schedule ‘M’, which is
the Indian version of cGMP norms of WHO was mooted in 2001 and notified in 2005. Given
that the Director General (Health Services) is the administrative authority under which
CRI, Kasauli and BCG VL, Chennai are functioning as subordinate offices, and office of
DCGI is the nodal agency entrusted with the responsibility of ensuring cGMP compliance at
PH Coonoor, it is the Ministry which should have made timely and appropriate efforts to
convert these age old structures as per Schedule M compliant standards. From the feedback
made available to the Committee, it can only conclude that no initiative was attempted for
drawing out an Action Plan for making these Institutes cGMP compliant. The Ministry’s
responsibility did not end with simply bringing out the required legislation in accordance
with the international norms. Rather, the real work was to begin thereafter which
unfortunately never happened. It is also not clear as to whether the Ministry has allocated
adequade funds to these Institutes for the purpose. The Committee also fails to understand
as to how the Ministry would ensure cGMP compliance in the private Institutes when it
cannot enforce the same in its own Institutes. (Para 5.2)
The Committee observes that the Ministry has failed to play the role of coordinator
and facilitator in the matter. It would like to draw attention to one such situation that
confirms its stand. From the Status note submitted by the Ministry, the Committee finds
that a proposal for converting the triple-vaccine manufacturing laboratory at CRI, Kasauli
into a cGMP compliant structure was made way back in 1997-98, when M/s  HSCC, Noida was
awarded the contract to build a cGMP compliant structure at CRI. However, the entire
exercise ended in a failure, as M/s HSCC, Noida, after continuing the exercise for nine
years and spending Rs. 11.86 crores of public money on the project, expressed its inability
and disinterest in completing the project in December, 2006. The Committee fails to
understand the logic why the Ministry waited so long in such a crucial matter. The
Committee feels that the Ministry should have taken immediate appropriate steps such as
canceling the contract of M/s HSCC, Noida and asked other parties with technical
competence to complete the project. It epitomizes the cavalier fashion with which the
Ministry has treated the issue. Only achievement seems to be an expenditure of Rs. 11.86
crores by M/s HSCC, Noida, without any specification thereof. The Committee views with
serious concern the admission on the part of M/s HSCC, Noida about their not having any
expertise to construct a scientific structure of cGMP standards. (Para 5.3)
15

16
The Committee was informed that a Departmental Inquiry in the matter was
presently going on. The Committee observes that this matter has been hanging on for more
than ten years. More than two years have elapsed since the Project authorities have
comfortably withdrawn themselves. The inquiry also seems to be continuing in a comfortable
mode. Nobody seems to be bothered about the loss of public money and also the institute
not getting the required renovation. The Committee would appreciate if the enquiry
proceedings are completed expeditiously and full details of follow up action taken for fixing
up the responsibility against the concerned official(s) in the Ministry and imposing of
penalty on the project authority are apprised to it. The Committee can only emphasise that
the major responsibility of making these Institutes cGMP compliant lies with the Ministry
and holding the Institutes entirely responsible for the same goes against the principle of
natural justice. The Committee is of the firm opinion that the Ministry is responsible to a
large extent for the prevailing unsatisfactory situation in all the three Institutes which
resulted in the cancellation of their vaccine producing licenses and thereby leading to
shortage of life saving vaccines with serious impact on Universal Immunization Programme
and child healthcare programmes in the country. (Para 5.4)
The Status Note also informs that the Institutes suffer from acute shortage of
personnel especially in Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ in CRI, Kasauli and BCG VL, Chennai which are
subordinate offices under the office of DGHS. The vacancies stated above are reflected in
percentage in the table given below:

BCG VL, Chennai 33 75 (Group ‘B’ Gazetted)
87.5 (Group ‘B’ Non-Gazetted)
(Para 5.5)
CRI, Kasauli has also stated that it has extreme shortage of scientists. It has also
reported that there have been no regular Director at the Institute after 1997 onwards and
also that the present incumbent is on deputation basis. A considerable number of vacancies
existed in the Technical Staff at the middle and the higher levels. The. Committee
understands that the power to fill up the vacancies in Group ‘A’ and Group ‘B’ posts in
these Institutes lies with the office of the Director General of Health Services and not the
Institutes. It is also clear from the information provided in the Status Report that the
Institutes had forwarded a number of proposals to the Ministry for filling up of vacancies
of group ‘A’ and ‘B’ services. But, it seems that the matter was not taken up in the right
earnest by the Ministry to fill up these vacancies. The Committee has also observed that
a number of posts have either lapsed/abolished or proposed to be lapsed/abolished. The
Committee would also like to state here that in comparison to CRI and BCG VL, the PII
which is an autonomous body functioning under the Ministry has not reported any shortage
of manpower. The Committee believes that if similar administrative autonomy had been
delegated to CRI and BCG VL, the problems relating to shortage of manpower and many
other such issues could have been sorted out early. The Committee would appreciate if a
work study about the staff requirement in accordance with GMP norms is initiated at the
earliest both at CRI and BCG VL so as to have a viable set up there. (Para 5.6)
The inspection report of the joint inspecting team points out that the there were 55

Institute has, in its Status report, informed that 45 deficiencies had already been rectified

17

justification for the existing position has been given by the institute. Not only this, the

Committee, the Institute had informed that rest of the rectification work had been unduly
delayed due to absence of a regular Director. The Director-In-Charge had not been vested

rectification work could not be issued by him. (Para 5.7)
The Committee was apprised that the Institute had informed the Deputy Drugs
Controller, South Zone on 26th February, 2008 and later on 20th March, 2008 to the

in the Institute. Also the Institute had preferred appeals twice—one on 24th January, 2008

does not mention as to what action was taken on the part of the Ministry to consider their
case in the light of the rectifications carried out by the Institute. (Para 5.8)
The Committee observes that out of 65 deficiencies pointed out by the Inspection

Director of such a premier institutions continues to be brought on deputation. One can well
imagine the state of affairs in an institute without a permanent Head for a prolonged
period. (Para 5.9)

Committee, it is evident that the Institute has admitted that while it would not be possible

manpower, the fact remains that these shor tfalls could have been easily tackled with the
support of the Ministry. (Para 5.10)
The Committee would also like to mention here that neither of the inspecting

down these units. (Para 5.11)

standards. The Committee observes that such lapses on the part of the Ministry only point

(Para 5.12)

18

“The Central Licensing Approving Authority may, after giving the licensee an

accordance with the law but also due to the fact that quite a few drawbacks have already

(i) Study of infrastructure facilities available at the three vaccine manufacturing

(ii) Scope of re-deployment of the existing staff in production units to the proposed

(Para 5.14)

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH
HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
2.4 The Committee notes that the overall allocation for the health sector (outside NRHM) has
been on the higher side. Still, the Committee is constrained to note that the Department has failed
to project its budgetary requirements in an effective way for the simple reason that the utilization
of funds during the Tenth Plan is far from satisfactory which is evident from the fact that the
sanctioned BE for 2005-06 and 2006-07 was Rs.4253.84 crores and Rs.3564.95 crores,
respectively, which was reduced to Rs.4096.25 crores and Rs.3433.02 crores, respectively at the
RE stage. The actual expenditure figures of Rs.2907.96 crores and Rs.3377.34 crores were even
less than the budgeted allocations at the RE stage. The Committee notes that this trend has
continued during 2007-08 also. This goes to illustrate that the Department’s record in utilization of
the allocated funds is below par. The Committee would, therefore, recommend the Department to
first ensure optimum and judicious utilization of the funds allocated instead of highlighting the
reduced budgetary allocation. The Committee also recommends to the Department to take
substantive steps so that the stumbling blocks in the utilization of sanctioned funds for 2008-09
for a crucial sector like health, are removed.
Action Taken
Noted for compliance.
Recommendations/Observations
2.7 Committee observes that in spite of its raising concerns over this trend of under utilization
of funds year after year, there does not seem to be any noticeable improvement in this regard. Time
and again the Committee has been advocating for higher allocation of funds for this sector and this
time the Committee is happy to note that the approved outlay has seen a 32% hike over the last
year’s Revised Estimate. The Committee reiterates its concern and recommends to the Department
to play a more pro-active role in identifying the problems afflicting the utilization of funds in the
Health Sector and initiate remedial measures from the very beginning of the current financial year so
that the old story of revising estimates downwards and subsequent under utilization does not recur.
Action Taken
Noted for compliance.

XI. PRADHAN MANTRI SWASTHYA SURAKSHA YOJANA (PMSSY)
Recommendations/Observations
11.6 The Committee in its 22nd Report on the Demands for Grants (2007-08) presented on
3rd May, 2007 had expressed its apprehension that it would take at least another plan period before
the six AIIMS like Institutions would start functioning in the real sense. The Committee is
constrained to modify its assessment. From the details made available to the Committee,
construction work on the Six AIIMS like Institutions is expected to start by August-
September, 2008 and would be completed in 24 months. Thus, it is more than clear now that only
buildings would be ready by the end of Eleventh Plan. The real target of making available best
health care services to public through these institutions seems to be a distant dream even now. The
Committee finds that tendering process for procurement of medical equipments is at an initial stage.
Process for other allied infrastructure facilities and manpower – both highly qualified/technical as
well as non-technical is yet so start. With regard to up gradation of 13 Medical College Institutions,
the Committee can only hope that work would be completed within the targeted date of 20 months.
The Committee is, however, worried about the fate of upgradation of Grants Medical College and
JJ hospital, Mumbai due to a court case pending in Nagpur High Court in the matter. The
Committee is of the view that the Department should take up other linked activities like arranging
for the faculty and requisite infrastructure simultaneously so that no delay takes place in
operationalization of the Institutions once the construction activity is completed.
Action Taken
Noted. The civil construction work is likely to be completed by the end of 2010. However,
parallel activities for procurement of medical equipment, manpower planning and recruitment,
finalization of governance and management structure as also preparation of curriculum design have
been initiated in 2008. The effort will be to make the hospital functional by the end of 2010 and
Medical College operational by academic year 2011.
Recommendations/Observations
11.7 The Committee also recommends that funds as and when required should be made available
to the Department. The Committee would, however, like to point out that though funds have never
been a problem for this ambitious project of national importance, utilization thereof has been far
from satisfactory level. The Committee, accordingly, recommends setting up of a joint mechanism
of Centre and the concerned States so that greater coordination is achieved and effective
monitoring of the ongoing projects is done. The Committee also calls for greater emphasis on
adhering to the time lines so that the overall cost of the project is not escalated further.

5
Action Taken
All out efforts are being made to fully utilize the funds allocated for the Project. A
Committee under the Chairmanship of Chief Secretaries of the concerned States is being set up to
monitor the progress of setting up of each of the six AIIMS-like institutions.
XII. IMPROVEMENT OF NURSING SERVICES
Recommendations/Observations
12.4 The Committee is not aware about the existence of any Monitoring Committee for such
projects. The Committee is of the view that such a mechanism will prove to be very useful,
especially in view of Rs.198.00 crores allocated for strengthening/upgradation of Nursing Services.
The Committee welcomes the enhancement in the assistance to be provided to Nursing
Institutions from Rs.10.00 lakhs to Rs.25.00 lakhs. Such a move was overdue. The Committee,
however, wonders whether any exercise has been initiated for identification of locations of all the
proposed Centres/Schools/Colleges so far. The Committee would appreciate if implementation of all
these projects is carried out in a time-bound manner. The Committee is not aware about any
assessment/review made recently about the (training both pre and in-service) programmes for
Nurses and also functioning of Training Institutions for Nurses. The Committee is of the view that
such an exercise is necessary for strengthening the Nursing Services which is a very crucial
component of health care.
Action Taken
Noted for compliance. The establishment of Monitoring and Evaluation Cell has been
proposed in the EFC Memo. Although no assessment has been made recently for pre and in-service
training and that of Training Institutions for Nurses but it is envisaged that the Monitoring and
Evaluation Cell when set up would take care of these aspects.
The enhanced grant of Rs.25.00 lakhs is meant for procurement of A.V. AIDS, laboratory
equipment, furniture, library, transport etc. and is need based and would be released to the nursing
institutions on the basis of proposals to be received from the states. Locations for establishing
Centres/Schools/Colleges have been identified. Details are at Annexure-XI.
Recommendations/Observations
12.5 The Committee is happy to note that the National Awards for Nurses, given as a mark of
highest recognition for the meritorious services of the nurses and nursing profession in the
Country, that continued up to 1989, have been revived and named as the National Florence
Nightingale Award from 2007 with the consent of the President of India. 17 Nursing personnel
have been awarded with this prestigious award during the year 2007.
Action Taken
The National Florence Nightingale Awards for the year 2008 have also been distributed by
the President of India to 26 meritorious nursing personnel in the award ceremony held on
12.5.2008 at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
Recommendations/Observations
12.6 The Committee recommends that a suitable mechanism should be evolved for maintaining
a live register of nurses so as to enable the Department for formulating appropriate policy
pertaining to nurses.

6
Action Taken
The Indian Nursing Council is already seized of the matter and will make efforts to devise
suitable mechanism to overcome the problem.
Recommendations/Observations
12.7 The Committee recommends that the Department should make all out efforts including
effective co-ordination and close monitoring so that all the proposals for strengthening of nursing
education are implemented properly and desired results are achieved for getting adequate number
of qualified and trained nursing personnel.
Action Taken
As regards effective coordination and monitoring of the project the Monitoring and
Evaluation Cell as explained in para 12.4 would take care of this aspect.
XV. NATIONAL URBAN HEALTH MISSION (NUHM)
Recommendations/Observations
15.4 The Committee observes that NUHM is one of the most ambitious Projects after National
Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are according to the
requirements of the present scenario. The Committee cautions the Department to take all necessary
steps so that the problems afflicting the implementation of NRHM like those related to ground level
healthcare functionaries, availability of doctors, paramedics and infrastructure do not recur and
interfere in the implementation of this parallel scheme meant for urban areas. For achieving the
targets proposed under mission, the Department should do proper homework and work out
modalities for their implementation. The Department should start coordinating with the States right
from the beginning of the project. The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress
made in this regard.
Action Taken
Based on the document on NUHM approved by Minister of Health and Family Welfare, a
draft EFC Memo for NUHM has been circulated to the concerned Ministries for seeking their view/
comments.
The EFC proposal envisages to achieve the objectives of NUHM by strengthening the
extents primary public health systems, rationalising the available manpower and resources, filling
the gaps in service delivery through private partnership through a regulatory frame work and also
through a communitised risk pooling/insurance mechanism with IT enablement, capacity building of
key stake holders and by making special provision for inclusion of the most vulnerable amongst
the poor.
All the State/UT Governments have been requested to start the work of GIS mapping of
the selected cities in TOP PRIORITY basis.
The teams of this Ministry has visited the States of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh
Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chandigarh UT, Haryana, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal,
Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand. A presentation on proposed NUHM and the GIS mapping was arranged
and the discussion was also held on various issues pertaining to the NUHM. The officials of
Puducherry were requested to come at Chennai and the officials of A&N Islands were requested
to come at Kolkata to participate in the meeting.

7
The teams would visit other States/UT Governments soon.

Recommendations/Observations

XXII. V ACANCIES IN CHS CADRE
Recommendations/Observations
22.5 The Committee views with serious concern the grave injustice done to the GDMO cadre
for no fault of theirs. Inspite of their being eligible for specialist post, continuance of such doctors
in GDMO cadre is indeed against all principles of natural justice. Non-implementation of Fifth Pay
Commission recommendation of SAG level positions in All India Service to be 17% of total cadre
has created another hurdle in their career progression. The Committee finds that Sixth Pay
Commission’s recommendations of filling up the additional posts to be created for fulfilling any gap,
by direct recruitment, will make the position of GDMOs very vulnerable. The Committee is of the
firm opinion that the Department should take up this issue immediately with the Ministry of
Finance. Every attempt should be made to remove the grave injustice done to the GDMO cadre
so that this sub-cadre of professionals gets due recognition and morale boost like others in All India
Services.
Action Taken
(i) In the new proposed CHS Rules, provision is being proposed for lateral entry of
General Duty Medical Officers with Post-graduate qualification in the Specialist
sub-cadre.
(ii) A proposal is under reference to COS for creating/upgrading 17% of total Senior Duty
posts in CHS for SAG level.

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
2.6 The Committee would like to point out that expenditure reported upto 29th February, 2008
was only Rs.1608.59 crores and within a span of three weeks it has reached to Rs.2121.24 crores.
This clearly indicates that major utilization is taking place in the last quarter of the year.
Action Taken
While this Ministry shares the views of the Committee, efforts are being made to streamline
the pace of expenditure as per Cash Management Plan.
Recommendations/Observations
2.8 The Committee views with serious concern the under utilization of funds on account of
slow pace of expenditure on implementation of schemes like Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha
Yojna (PMSSY), Cancer, Mental Health, Capacity Building Project for Food and Drugs, non-
implementation of the recommendations of the Oversight Committee, New Initiatives, and also non-
finalizations of proposals relating to procurement of various equipments, non-filling up of vacant
posts, non-receipt of proposals from State Government/Implementing Agencies etc. The Committee
recommends the Department to keep the activities of these schemes/institutions under constant
monitoring so as to arrest this trend of under utilization.
Action Taken
The concern of the Committee is fully shared by the Ministry. Implementation of the
schemes mentioned is being accordingly monitored on a regular basis by Secretary (H&FW) and
in the context of the observations of the Committee will be examined for such action as considered
necessary to ensure proper utilization of funds.
Recommendations/Observations

29th February, 2008 is a meagre 14.13 crores. A proposal for releasing funds to the extent of

Action Taken
According to the Tenth Plan Scheme of the National Mental Health Programme, all the
proposals for extending District Mental Health Programme, Upgradation of Psychiatric Wings of
Government Medical Colleges/General Hospitals and Modernisation of Government Mental Hospitals

Secretary (Health and FW) for approval. Besides, approval of IFD is also obtained in the matter.

Governments/Institutions. Non-receipt of adequate number of complete proposals in time from the

State Governments have been held. A review meeting on NMHP with the State Health Secretaries/
Directors of Health Services/Nodal Officers was held in February, 2007. A meeting was also held

alia, discussed. Regional Meetings were held during August-September, 2007 with the State Nodal
Officers for NMHP to review progress of implementation of the Programme. Review meetings on
the implementation of NMHP were also held on 3rd March and 25th March, 2008. All the
representatives of State Governments were requested to submit proposals for assistance under
various components of the Programme and to submit financial year-wise Utilisation Certificates
along with Audited Statements
In order to overcome these problems, it has been envisaged in the EFC Proposal on NMHP
for implementation during the Eleventh  Five Year Plan, to decentralize the programme and also to
integrate it with National Rural Health Mission. Grants under different schemes to a particular State
would be released through the State Health Society along with the schemes and guidelines for
NMHP. S tate Nodal Of ficer representing the programme in the State Health Society would get the
grants released for various districts and institutions. At the district level, the Programme Officer
would represent the programme in the District Health Society and facilitate operationalisation of
DMHP.
A proposal for releasing funds to the extent of Rs.22.165 crore through the State Health
Societies was under consideration but this could not materialize, as the I.F.D./competent authority

programme envisaged for the Eleventh Plan is yet to be approved. The Committee recommends to

34

For effective and efficient implementation of the programme, periodical interactions with the

XXIII. NEW SCHEMES
Recommendations/Observations
23.2 The Committee is dismayed to note that every year the Department announces new
schemes/programmes, many of which are without finalizing the modalities and proper ground work,
thereby resulting in under or no utilization of funds. The Committee recommends to the Department
to enhance its efforts to complete all necessary formalities and launch the programmes at the

Action Taken
Most of the Schemes were introduced during 2007-08 It being the first year for
implementation, there was slow progress in appraisal/approval of the schemes which slowed down
the pace of expenditure. The implementation process has gradually gained momentum and the
progress in this regard for certain schemes is given as follows:—
• Pilot project on Prevention and Control of Human Rabies.
• Leptospirosis Control Programme.
The two projects, initially envisaged for five years have been revised in consultation with
Integrated Finance Division and approval of the competent authority has now been obtained to
carry out the projects on pilot basis for two years only.
Project on Prevention and Control of Human Rabies is being carried out on pilot basis in
four cities, namely Delhi, Ahmedabad, Bangalore and Pune, whereas Leptospirosis Control
Programme is to be carried out on pilot basis in three States.
The strategy for implementation of the respective pilot projects has been firmed up and the
action plans have also been drawn for the current year. Nodal Officers in pilot cities/States have
been identified and Core Groups have also been constituted for implementation of the projects.
Draft MoU are under progress. Terms of Reference for appointment of Consultants and Data Entry
Operators under the projects have been formulated. Proforma for collection of base line data and
also for surveillance of respective diseases have been finalized and circulated to the concerned
cities/States. Steps are being taken to strengthen the laboratories and for preparation of IEC
material.
• National Organ Transplant Programme – The National Organ Transplant Programme is
at an advanced stage of formulation. The programme is to be proceeded by
amendments in the THOA Acts and Rules. The amended rules have been notified. The
Cabinet note for amending the THOA is under circulation to concerned Ministries.
• Oral Health – While the Ministry has been in the process of preparing an EFC proposal
for the programme, the Ministry of Finance issued instructions in June, 2008 to the
effect that no new scheme/programme should be launched in the current financial year
even if Budget provision has been made for the same unless it has been mentioned in

36
the Finance Minister’s Budget Speech for 2008-09. As this programme was not
mentioned in the Finance Minister’s Budget Speech, further action in the matter was
held in abeyance.
Nevertheless, in the meeting of Senior Officers under the chairmanship of Secretary
(H&FW) held on 19th August, 2008, it was decided to merge this programme with
National Rural Health Mission. Ministry is in the process of examining the proposal
from this angle, to finalise those parts of the Scheme that can be merged with NRHM.

for Health Care for Elderly has been submitted to IFD.
• National Centre for Disease Control – Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in view
of emerging and re-emerging of infectious diseases and rapid response thereto,
proposed to transform National Institute of Communicable Diseases into National
Centre for Disease Control (NCDC). During discussions with Planning Commission on
the EFC note for the proposal, it was suggested that an Independent appraisal of the
Institution should be undertaken and DPR should be prepared. Accordingly, appraisal
of the institute has been conducted by IIT, Delhi. Further, Consultant for Bid Process

submitted.

Safdarjung Hospital has been approved. Work is held up on account of litigation
involving the State and Centre.
• National Advisory Board of Standards – National Advisory Board for Standards has
already started functioning.
XXIV. MISCELLANEOUS
Recommendations/Observations
24.2 The Committee recommends the Department to work out modalities for establishing
specialized kidney centers immediately and in the mean time approach the Planning Commission for
funds with a proposal to improve dialysis facility in the country. In view of increasing gap in
demand and supply, at least the well known Institutes across India should be provided with the
dialysis machines during the current financial year. The Committee would like to be informed about
the steps taken by the Department in this regard.
Action Taken
There is shortage of Dialysis facilities in the country. Health is state subject and it is for
state Government concerned to provide the health care facilities to the general public. There is
shortage of qualified doctors to run the dialysis machines. There are very few centres which are
providing D.M. (Nephrology) super specialty courses and there are about 500 such specialities in
the country. Curriculum for training of physicians for dialysis is being finalised in collaboration with
IGNOU with a view to start short term training programmes to bridge the gap. Efforts are being
made to initiate the standalone dialysis in the CGHS Delhi. In this regard, some proposals are under
consideration and expert opinion has been taken. Till such time, CGHS patients are reimbursed the
money spent by beneficiaries on Dialysis in the private sector. Similarly other organised sector and

37
Government employees who are covered under similar insurance schemes namely CS (MA) and
ESI are provided the reimbursement.
Central Government institutions e.g. AIIMS, PGI, JIPMER, RML Hospital and Safdarjung
Hospital are already having Dialysis facilities and further upgradation is done from time to time.
There is decentralised decision making in the Health Care Delivery System under National Rural
Health System and State Governments can require equipments themselves.
National Organ Transplant Programme is being finalised and likely to be initiated soon.

III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS)
Recommendations/Observations
3.5 The Committee would like to point out that situation is some what different. Problems are
being faced both by the CGHS functionaries and beneficiaries. Technicians, Junior staff manning
counters in dispensaries and attending doctors need to be fully trained. Practical problems like
internet and electricity failure have to be tackled by having an alternative arrangement. These initial
teething problems should not be allowed to be prolonged. At present, beneficiaries which include
senior citizens also are being made to wait for hours at the dispensaries. Their ordeal starts right
from the registration counter and continues upto delivery of medicines. The Committee would
appreciate if all the measures including training, smooth running of computers with full
connectivity, backup for power failure are taken at the earliest and also closely monitored.
Action Taken
The Speed of Internet has improved w.e.f. 1st April 2008. After discussing with MTNL
Internet speed has been enhanced to 2mbps at dispensaries with effect from 1.4.2008.
NIC has also strengthened the Computer servers to improve better connectivity. The
support of Data Entry Operators at Dispensaries is continuing. MTNL has identified Nodal officers
specifically to address the internet related complaints of CGHS dispensaries. NIC has also
earmarked eight Supervisors to take care of software related problems at dispensaries. The project
is closely monitored by Additional Directors, CGHS, Director, CGHS, Sr. Technical Director, NIC
and Senior Officers of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. In addition regular meetings are held
with officials of MTNL.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee had called for taking measures which includes training of the staff,
connectivity of the computer systems and their backup for power failure. However, the
Department has concentrated on the aspect of internet related issues, viz., enhancing its
speed and software related problems. The issue of training of staff and the power backup
seems to have been ignored at this juncture. The Committee would like to emphasize that
though internet efficiency is a vital aspect of the computerization programme, yet it has to
be seen in totality. The issue of proper training of the staff and the power backup are also
crucial for the success of the computerization exercise. The Committee, therefore, expects
the Department to chalk out a proper strategy in this regard.
Recommendations/Observations
3.6 The Committee has been emphasizing for long for introduction of two shift system in
CGHS. The Committee does not appreciate the contention of the Ministry that a large number of
private hospitals and diagnostic centres have been empanelled under the CGHS and in case of
emergency, beneficiaries can go there for treatment and claim re-imbursement later. The Committee
would like to draw the attention of the Ministry once again to the fact that idea behind having two
shifts in CGGS dispensaries is the inconvenience being faced by the CGHS beneficiaries, majority
of them office goers in going to the dispensaries in the morning hours. The Committee is disturbed

42
by the element of helplessness shown by the Ministry in their candid admission of staff side
vehemently opposing the move. In this era where the service providers like banks etc. are opting
for flexible timings to give their customers maximum possible services, at least the Ministry could
have come forward with a positive and proactive approach. The Committee would reiterate its
recommendation made last year for starting two shifts in a few dispensaries as a test case. One
must not forget that CGHS is a service oriented scheme, supposedly providing health care mainly
to our serving employees and pensioners. It is the responsibility of the Ministry to make the CGHS
employees understand and not to be pressurized by them.
Action Taken
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare intends to take the matter before the Committee
of Secretaries.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee observes that its recommendation regarding starting of two shifts
system in CGHS dispensaries has ultimately resulted in a positive response from the
Department. The Committee would appreciate if the matter is placed before the Committee
of Secretaries at the earliest.

already available should start at the earliest. All procedural formalities should be expedited and

in Dwarka. The Department has in its recent update had admitted that it had been allotted
three plots of land in Dwarka at Sectors 6, 8 and 12. The problem cited here is that the

Action Taken
The World Bank had conducted a Detailed Implementation Review (DIR) in 2006-07 for the
period 1999-2006 for the bank funded health sector projects, including the National AIDS Control
Programme Phase II. The bank had raised issues related to the selection of NGOs in Maharashtra,
Karnataka, Orissa and Chhattisgarh, inadequate monitoring and possibility of bribery and instances
where equipment for blood banks and diagnostic kits were not as per laid down guidelines. Many
of the allegations were anecdotal based on ‘confidential information’. The DIR report did not have
evidence or relevant material on individual persons who could be held responsible for malafide
reasons. The shortcomings noticed were systemic in nature. NACO took a detailed review and
senior officers visited the States. As there appeared to be some evidence of corruption by the then
Project Directors of Chhattisgarh and Karnataka, the matter has been referred to the CBI.
Many of the shortcomings mentioned in the DIR had already been addressed in NACP Phase
III and revised guidelines prepared in consultation with national experts, World Bank and other
donors. It is agreed that there were shortcomings in procurement in so far as the World Bank
procedures were concerned and action was initiated in consultation with World Bank officials.
These steps were taken to strengthen existing systems to ensure transparency and equity and
minimize potential areas of fraud and corruption. These activities were started well before the DIR
report.
Development of detailed guidelines and operational manuals for procurement of

III. INFRASTRUCTURE STRENGTHENING
Recommendations/Observations
3.1 NRHM aims at strengthening of Primary Health Infrastructure and improving effective
service delivery across the country. Sub-centres, Primary Healthcare Centres and Community
Health Centres are the three pillars on which rural infrastructure is built. As on March, 2007, there
are 1,45,272 Sub-Centres, 22,370 PHCs and 4045 CHCs in the country. There is a shortfall of
20,855 Sub-Centres, 6491 PHCs and 2525 CHCs in the country based on the 2001 population
norms. The Committee has been constantly drawing the attention of the Department to the uneven
spread of these centres across the country with prominent gaps in the High Focus States. The
Committee finds that there is no marked improvement in this regard.
The Committee has been expressing its serious concern on the continuance of lack of rural
health infrastructure, especially in the High Focus States where the need is the most. On being
asked to identify the problem areas, the Committee has been informed that health infrastructure and
allocation of health workers under NRHM is planned on the population, work load and distance
norms. Shortages on the basis of 2001 population are quantified as the difference between the
required number of facilities/providers as per the norms and those that are functioning or in
position. This method of determining norms and shortage does not take into account the varying
epidemiological, geographical and socio-demographic patterns across the different States/
communities and between rural and urban areas within States. The actual availability of different
types of providers or the extent of private/voluntary sector involvement in healthcare delivery at
the community level is also not taken into account. The Committee notes that against the backdrop
of these very visible deficiencies, norms for setting up of the Sub-Centres and PHCs have been
modified by the Steering Committee of the Planning Commission. These norms to be adopted
during the Eleventh Plan have been duly approved by the Planning Commission also. The
Committee has been given to understand that population-centric norms are replaced with flexible
norms comprising habitation-based needs, community based needs and disease-pattern based needs.
Action Taken
The core objective of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) is to strengthen primary
healthcare infrastructure for effective service delivery especially in the rural areas. Acknowledging
the limitation of a population centric norm, NRHM has provided for construction of health facilities
based on caseload, distance and other criterions. Construction of Sub-Centres, PHC, CHC etc. have
been taken up from NRHM funds as well as Finance Commission funds released to States. The
suggestion of the Planning Commission has also been taken cognizance of by the Ministry.
V. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendations/Observations
5.4 The Committee appreciates the successful implementation of RNTCP Phase-I and ongoing
Phase-II. Several initiatives/interventions taken at different levels and variety of implementing
64

65
agencies have contributed to the increasing population coverage and 85% cure rate. However, India
still contributes 20% of TB cases reported in the world. Out of 8.8 million cases per annum, 1.8
million cases are from India alone. New complex offshoots of TB also keep on emerging, the most
visible being worsening HIV epidemic increasing the number of TB cases. The Committee notes
that HIV is the most potent risk factor for progression of TB infection to disease form HIV-TB
patients detected in 2005 were 12,062, 13,614 in 2006 and 18,559 in 2007. The Committee is
aware that increase in number of co-infected (HIV–TB) patients being detected over the last three
years is a result of innovative and coordinated measures taken by the Department. But the other
dimension of this trend is increasing complexities involved in the treatment of such cases. The
Committee hopes that the National Framework formulated by RNTCP and NACP for joint TB/HIV
collaborative activities will lead to better and effective control of this emerging problem area.
Action Taken
With increasing number of HIV infected TB patients being routinely detected by the
cross-referral mechanisms between RNTCP and NACP, the programmes have prioritized providing
access to HIV care to the co-infected patients.
The Central TB Division, in collaboration with NACO, has successfully piloted a mechanism
for decentralized delivery of CPT to HIV infected TB patients through RNTCP and referral of all
such cases to nearest NACP ART Centre, where these patients would be promptly provided
monthly supplies of ART. These interventions have been included in the National framework for
joint TB/HIV collaborative activities and would be implemented in the country in a phased manner.
Recommendations/Observations
5.5 The Committee observes that the other major challenge to TB control in the country is
increasing number of MDR-TB cases. The Committee is aware that such cases are bound to
increase the magnitude and severity of TB epidemic and pose a major threat to TB control. The
Committee in its earlier Report has pointed out that 7% defaulters in a year is quite a significant
number of cases remaining untreated or half-treated. With a single TB patient infecting 10-15
persons in a year, rate of infection is bound to increase. The Committee would like to point out
that formulation of guidelines for management of MDR-TB cases and publication thereof will not
prove to be sufficient. The Committee had given a simple suggestion for identifying the defaulter
TB patients from the records being maintained at centres/hospitals with the help of NGOs/Social
Workers and Private Practitioners. Intention of the Committee was to identify such cases at the
first default stage itself. The Committee finds that under a new initiative a total of 50 MDR-TB
patients were to be registered for treatment in Gujarat and Maharashtra during 2007-08 and to be
doubled every year subsequently and ultimately in the entire country. While welcoming this
initiative, the Committee would also like to point out that cost of MDR-TB treatment is 300 times
more than non-MDR TB. The Committee can only say that preventive measures will be both cost-
effective and helpful for the patients. The Committee is of the firm opinion that through effective
IEC activities and alertness of health workers, regular intake of medicines can be easily monitored.
The Committee, therefore, suggests that in monitoring of TB patients the most vital aspect should
not be ignored at any cost.
Action Taken
The Ministry agrees with the observation of the Committee that measures to prevent the
development of MDR-TB will be both cost-effective and helpful for the patients. In consonance
with this spirit, the key focus of the programme is to make sure that the patients complete their
treatment as per schedule and on default the retrieval actions are taken immediately. Thus emphasis

66
of the programme is to implement quality DOTS to achieve highest cure rates and prevent MDR
TB.
The programme is laying lot of stress on ensuring provision of anti-TB drugs under the
direct observation. This aspect is covered during the modular training as well as reinforced during
supervisory visits and also during internal evaluations.
The RNTCP views management of MDR TB as a ‘standard of care’ issue and has identified
the following challenges and is addressing them on a priority basis:
• Minimizing default from treatment.
• Ensuring accurate categorization of previously treated patients as Category-II.
• Ensuring reliable DOT throughout treatment.
• Improve re-treatment success through intensified support, supervision, and monitoring
of DOT in category II patients through involvement of NGOs, PPs and Community
V olunteers.
• Improving Public-Private Mix (PPM) activities and uptake of DOTS by private sector
and medical colleges.
The Ministry agrees with the views of the Committee and focuses its highest priority to
reduce the default among TB patients through constant monitoring, involvement of NGOs, other
sectors and creating awareness through IEC activities.

from the organizers before granting permission to them for conducting Eye Screening Camps.
Now, Eye Screening Camps are allowed but the Eye operations in the camps have been banned
by Government of India due to high rate of mishaps in such camps w.e.f. 1997.
Recommendations/Observations
7.9 The Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the findings of a survey on Rapid
Assessment of TRACHOMA cases done in the district of Haryana, Gujarat, U.P., Uttarakhand,
Punjab and Rajasthan. Findings of this survey were that against the popular perception of there
being no transmission of trachoma cases in India, all districts showed active cases.
The Committee notes with disappointment that the target to bring prevalence of blindness to
0.8% by 2007 has not been reached. The Department has informed that as per the report of Rapid
Survey on Avoidable Blindness (2007), the prevalence of blindness has come down to 1% and that
Cataract remains the single largest cause of blindness, low vision and one eye blindness in India. The
Committee also infers from the above study that the prevalence of blindness due to Trachoma also
continues to be there. It is a well known fact that blindness is a bane of nature. The Committee
believes that most of the people in smaller towns and rural areas are not aware of the symptoms
of the above ailments, and the methods to manage eye care, hence their eye-care service seeking
behavior pattern do not change. The Committee exhorts the Department to take all possible necessary
steps to devise IEC activities in local media and television channels so that awareness among the
people is increased. The Committee believes a lot of cases of blindness can be checked by such a
measure and would in the long run help to achieve the targeted goals under the programme.
Action Taken
On the basis of findings of the Survey on Rapid Assessment of TRACHOMA about
presence of Trachoma cases in some pockets of some States in the country, IEC activities for
public awareness about Trachoma have been intensified through electronic media such as Radio,
Television, print and press media etc. The guidelines in this regard have also been issued to States
including NE States. Spots on TV and Radio have been produced in regional languages also.

proposed by the Planning Commission was called for. The Committee is, however, not aware
whether any preparatory exercise has been initiated for conducting surveys as per the revised
norms. The Committee is afraid that if this issue is allowed to linger on for long, the very objective
of NRHM of bridging gaps in the health care will continue to be a distant dream. The Committee,

KALA-AZAR
Recommendations/Observations
4.9 The Committee has been observing increasing trend of Kala-azar cases. In 2006, 39178
cases and 187 deaths were reported with 162 deaths occurring in Bihar alone. Position seems to
have worsened further in 2007. Upto November, 2007, already 35,638 cases with 158 deaths have
been reported. State-wise figures upto May, 2007 indicate that out of 79 deaths reported till then,
64 deaths have occurred in Bihar. While the Committee would not dispute the Department’s stand
that intensive surveillance has led to reporting of increased number of cases, the fact remains that
treatment compliance of Kala-azar cases detected is far from satisfactory in view of alarming rate
of deaths being reported. Number of initiatives for Kala-azar elimination undertaken seem to have
made no impact with ground reality continuing to be as discouraging as before. The Committee
understands that 200 villages of 9 districts reporting large number of Kala-azar cases have been
selected for focused interventions.
The Committee strongly feels that effective surveillance, timely treatment and compliance of
treatment regimens in all PRCs can perhaps lead to better reports in 2008. The Committee is of the

Recommendations/Observations
5.9 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by Studies like Social Assessment Study,
Institutional Assessment Study in respect of TB Control measures undertaken so far. The Committee
would like to point out that TB infection is no more confined to the poor and marginalized sections
of the society. Growing number of patients now belong to middle class and also affluent population.
There is an urgent need for making an analysis of basic factors behind this emerging situation which
can ultimately reach to alarming proportions. The Committee hopes that with the availability of both
funds and manpower, the Department will take up such an exercise at the earliest.
Action Taken
Survey undertaken by TB Research Centre, Chennai (TRC) has shown that the prevalence
of TB is around 4 times higher amongst the lower socio-economic strata as compared to the
higher. However, TB being an airborne infection, can affect individuals from any of the socio-
economic groups. Studies indicate that some of the other key predisposing factors, besides
overcrowding and malnutrition, include smoking, diabetes, HIV co-infection etc. which cut across
all the socio-economic groups. The most effective way to achieve TB control is to cut the
transmission of infection by early diagnosis and prompt treatment of all TB patients. The
programme is hence focusing on providing quality assured diagnostic and treatment services which
are easily accessible to all the sections of the community. The programme has plans to repeat the
social assessment study during the current phase of RNTCP project wherein some of these factors
would be evaluated.

Matter of Record.

complex and well away from ground realities when one finds that only remuneration payable to
